explanations.answer: Whether the LORD is still in Zion
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The cry asks, “Is the LORD no longer in Zion? Is her King no longer there?” (Jeremiah 8:19). I think it sounds like someone calling from far away who can't see Him anywhere. That's a lonely question, friend.

explanations.answer: Whether Egypt will send them help
explanations.explanation: Egypt never comes up in this cry. The people are calling out “from a land far away,” and what they ask is about the LORD: “Is the LORD no longer in Zion?” It's less a request for backup and more a question about where He is. I think that makes it hit harder.

explanations.answer: Whether the rain will ever return
explanations.explanation: Rain isn't what they're asking about, friend. The cry comes “from a land far away,” and the question is, “Is the LORD no longer in Zion? Is her King no longer there?” That's a question about the LORD Himself. Nobody in this verse is checking the weather.

Idols it is. The LORD asks, “Why have they provoked Me to anger with their carved images, with their worthless foreign idols?” (Jeremiah 8:19). He names them twice in one breath, carved images and foreign idols. He wants it understood where the anger is pointing.

Not enemies, friend. In this question the LORD points at the people's own “carved images” and “worthless foreign idols.” Enemies show up elsewhere in the chapter, but this question aims at what His people made and bowed to. That's the thing He says provoked Him.

Sacrifices aren't mentioned in this question. The LORD says they provoked Him “with their carved images, with their worthless foreign idols.” So the blank is idols. It's a short verse, so it's easy to blink and miss the answer sitting right there.

Not quite, friend. The line says, “The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved.” That “but” is the whole turn. It's like the oven timer going off and the batch still isn't done. The season is over and the rescue hasn't come.

Right, it's false. The verse says, “The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved.” Time keeps moving and the saving hasn't arrived. It sounds like people who've waited out a whole season for help and are still waiting.

explanations.answer: Why the people still aren't healed
explanations.explanation: You caught it. The speaker asks, “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no physician there?” and then asks, “Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?” (Jeremiah 8:22). The medicine and the doctor are right there in the question. The real ache is that the healing hasn't come.

explanations.answer: Who will pay for the medicine
explanations.explanation: Nobody mentions money in this verse, friend. The speaker points to the balm and the physician, then asks, “Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?” So the question underneath is why the people still aren't healed. No bill in sight.

explanations.answer: When Gilead will send its army
explanations.explanation: No armies in this verse. Gilead comes up for its balm and its physician: “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no physician there?” Then the speaker asks why the health of his people hasn't been restored. It's a question about healing, friend.

explanations.answer: A traveler's lodge to leave his people
explanations.explanation: That's the wish. He says, “If only I had a traveler's lodge in the wilderness, I would abandon my people and depart from them…” (Jeremiah 9:2). That's a big turn after all those tears. I think he's worn all the way down.

explanations.answer: A quiet place to pray for his people
explanations.explanation: That sounds sweet, but it isn't what he says. He wishes for “a traveler's lodge in the wilderness,” and then says, “I would abandon my people and depart from them.” The wish is about leaving, not praying. I think it shows how heavy things have gotten for him.

explanations.answer: A well to bring his people water
explanations.explanation: No well here, friend. Water shows up in the verse before, where he wishes his head were a spring of water and his eyes a fountain of tears. In this verse he wishes for “a traveler's lodge in the wilderness” so he could “depart from them.” The wish is about getting away.

That's the reason the verse gives. He says, “for they are all adulterers, a crowd of faithless people.” That's a hard thing to say about your own people. It comes right after tears, so I think this man loves them and is still worn out by what he sees.
The verse doesn't say that, friend. His reason is, “for they are all adulterers, a crowd of faithless people.” Nobody in the passage laughs at his tears. The faithlessness is what he points to.
Nothing in the verse says that. He gives one reason: “for they are all adulterers, a crowd of faithless people.” So his wish to leave comes from their faithlessness. His family's land never comes up.

Right. The LORD says, “Let everyone guard against his neighbor…” (Jeremiah 9:4). When lies prevail over truth in the land, even a neighbor gets handled with care. It's a sad picture. Folks keep one eye open around the people next door.
No elders show up in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “Let everyone guard against his neighbor…” That's the instruction. It isn't about taking anybody anywhere.
That's not what this verse says. Here the LORD says, “Let everyone guard against his neighbor…” With lies everywhere, the word is to be on guard. It's a very different mood from forgiving.

Not this time, friend. The LORD says, “do not trust any brother, for every brother deals craftily, and every friend spreads slander.” Brothers don't get a pass. Even family and friends are on the list.

Right, it's false. The LORD says, “do not trust any brother, for every brother deals craftily, and every friend spreads slander.” The warning covers the neighbor, the brother and the friend. It's a land where trust has worn very thin.
That's it. The LORD says, “in their deceit they refuse to know Me” (Jeremiah 9:6). The word is refuse, friend. They live in the middle of deception, and they won't know Him.
The Sabbath isn't in this verse. The LORD says, “in their deceit they refuse to know Me.” What they refuse is to know Him. That's the heart of the matter here.
Wages don't come up here, friend. The LORD says, “in their deceit they refuse to know Me.” So what they refuse is to know the LORD. Everything else in this verse hangs on that.

That's what He says. “Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do because of the daughter of My people?” (Jeremiah 9:7). Notice the question tucked inside, “what else can I do.” I think that sounds like someone with a heavy heart.

explanations.answer: Give them a brand new king
explanations.explanation: No new king in this verse, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, “I will refine them and test them.” Then He asks what else He can do because of His people. That's all the verse gives us.

explanations.answer: Bring them home from far away
explanations.explanation: That's not in this verse. The LORD of Hosts says, “I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do because of the daughter of My people?” A cry from a land far away does show up earlier, in verse 8:19. But here, what He says He'll do is refine and test.
Yes. “With his mouth a man speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he sets a trap for him.” Sweet words on the outside, a trap on the inside. That's the deception the LORD keeps pointing at.

That would be nice, friend, but the verse goes the other way. “With his mouth a man speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he sets a trap for him.” The peace is only on his lips. His heart is busy with a trap.

Repaying isn't in the verse. It says, “With his mouth a man speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he sets a trap for him.” The text gives no reason for the trap. It just shows the gap between the mouth and the heart.

Not so, friend. The LORD asks, “Should I not punish them for these things?” and then, “Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this?” (Jeremiah 9:9). He does not say He'll overlook it. It's a heavy verse.

Right, it's false. The LORD asks, “Should I not punish them for these things?” and then, “Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this?” He doesn't say He'll let it slide. It's a heavy moment, and the passage doesn't hurry past it.

explanations.answer: They've been scorched and left empty
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The mountains and pasture “have been scorched so no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard.” So the weeping comes from the scorched, empty land. It's a quiet picture, and a sad one.

explanations.answer: A great flood has covered them
explanations.explanation: No flood in this verse, friend. The land has “been scorched so no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard.” Fire and dryness, not water. The weeping is over land that has gone empty.

explanations.answer: Strangers have fenced them all off
explanations.explanation: Nobody fences anything in this verse. The mountains and pasture “have been scorched so no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard.” Scorched and empty is the reason for the weeping.
True. The verse says, “Both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled; they have gone away.” No cattle lowing, no birds, no beasts. That's an empty land.

It's true, friend. The verse says, “Both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled; they have gone away.” Even the animals are gone from that scorched land. That tells you how empty it has become.
